questions.q: Which condition defines a process {X_t} as a martingale with respect to filtration {F_t}?
options: Var(X_t) = Var(X_s) for all s < t
E[X_t | F_s] = X_s for all s < t
X_t is independent of X_s for all s < t
X_t must always be increasing
questions.explain: The martingale property requires that the conditional expectation of the future value, given all information up to time s, equals the current value X_s — no predictable drift in either direction.

questions.q: Why is standard Brownian motion W_t a martingale?
options: Because W_t is always positive
Because W_t − W_s is independent of F_s and has mean zero, so E[W_t | F_s] = W_s + E[W_t − W_s] = W_s
Because Brownian motion never changes value
Because W_t has a nonzero deterministic drift
questions.explain: Conditioning on F_s and using that the future increment is independent of the past with zero mean gives E[W_t|F_s] = W_s, satisfying the martingale property exactly.

questions.q: If a stock follows GBM dS_t = μS_t dt + σS_t dW_t under the real-world measure P with μ > 0, is S_t a martingale under P?
options: Yes, always, regardless of μ
No — E[S_t | F_s] = S_s·e^{μ(t−s)}, which exceeds S_s whenever μ > 0, so S_t drifts upward and is not a P-martingale
Yes, because all asset prices are martingales under every measure
No, because stock prices can never be modeled with GBM
questions.explain: With positive drift μ, the conditional expectation of the future price grows exponentially relative to the current price, violating the martingale condition under the real-world measure P.

questions.q: What does the fundamental theorem of asset pricing state about the risk-neutral measure Q?
options: Q makes the raw, undiscounted price process a martingale
A market is arbitrage-free if and only if there exists an equivalent measure Q under which the discounted asset price e^{-rt}S_t is a martingale
Q only applies to bonds, never to stocks
Q eliminates all randomness from asset prices
questions.explain: The fundamental theorem of asset pricing links the absence of arbitrage to the existence of a measure Q under which discounted prices (not raw prices) are martingales.

questions.q: In the Monte Carlo check of the discounted GBM price, why is the risk-free rate r used as the drift instead of the stock's real-world expected return μ?
options: Because r and μ are always numerically equal in practice
Because the simulation is meant to verify the martingale property under the risk-neutral measure Q, where the drift is replaced by r specifically so that e^{-rt}S_t has constant expectation
Because using μ would make the simulation run faster
Because r is always larger than μ
questions.explain: The martingale property for the discounted price only holds under the risk-neutral measure Q, which is defined by replacing the real-world drift μ with the risk-free rate r. Simulating with μ instead would not produce a flat discounted expectation.
